title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Perdone + , + creo que hay un problema

rules.text: doler is built exactly like gustar: the part that hurts is the SUBJECT and the verb agrees with it — me duele la cabeza, me duelen los pies. me only says who feels it. gustar was never a quirk; it is a class.
The article stands where English wants a possessive: me duele LA cabeza, never mi cabeza. The me has already said whose it is.
tener que plus a dictionary-form verb is how Spanish says "have to": tengo que ir. The que cannot be dropped, and tengo ir is not a sentence.
Spanish complains through the frame, not through volume: Perdone, creo que hay un problema. An unsoftened No funciona reads as an accusation, and softening it takes two words.
problema is masculine despite the -a, because it is one of a small Greek family — el problema, el tema. It is the promise M1 of the level below made when it refused the "-o/-a" shortcut.

words.note: doler, and the stem changes o→ue exactly as poder does. The thing that hurts is the subject, so one thing takes duele and more than one takes duelen.
Feminine: la cabeza. The z is the same th or s as in cerca, depending where you are.

sentences.trap: The head is doing the hurting, not you. That is why the verb agrees with it and not with the person who feels it.
sentences.sound: DWE-le, with the same glide as puedo. ka-BE-sa or ka-BE-tha.

variations.changed: M7's le, so it is someone else who feels it
asked of a friend
no in front of the pronoun and the verb alike

mistake.why: The me already says whose head it is: me duele la cabeza.

sentences.usage: The commonest complaint anyone makes, and the frame carries every other one.
sentences.mnemonic: The body part does the hurting; you only receive it.

words.note: Two feet, so the verb goes plural — because the feet are the subject. The row for doler is S01's.
Masculine: los pies. The singular is pie, one syllable.

sentences.trap: me does not change for the plural and the verb does. It is exactly the me gusta / me gustan pair from the first module of the course.
sentences.sound: DWE-len, and PYES as a single syllable.

variations.changed: mucho on the verb, where it belongs
someone else feeling it
the question, to a friend

mistake.why: The feet are the subject and there are two of them: me duelen.

sentences.usage: After a long day walking, which in a Spanish city is most of them.
sentences.mnemonic: Count the body parts, not the people.

words.note: Masculine: el teléfono. The accent marks the stress two syllables from the end, which is unusual and therefore written.
Of a machine only. A person who works is trabaja, and the two are never swapped.

sentences.trap: funcionar is for machines and trabajar is for people. English uses "work" for both and Spanish will not.
sentences.sound: te-LE-fo-no, four syllables, stressed where the accent says.

variations.changed: something bigger than a phone
the subject dropped, as Spanish does once it is known
asked as a question, subject at the end

mistake.why: trabajar is what a person does for a living. A machine funciona.

sentences.usage: Reporting a fault. On its own it is flat; S07 shows how to soften it.

words.note: Describes the state something is in, so it goes with estar and agrees with the thing: la puerta está rota.

sentences.trap: estar, not ser. Being broken is a state, and ser would be claiming the thing is broken by nature.
sentences.sound: RO-to, with the initial r rolled — a single tap is a different word.

variations.changed: a feminine thing, so the adjective moves
the module's own object

variations.cue: It isn't broken, it just doesn't work.
variations.changed: the two complaints set against each other

mistake.why: A state takes estar: está roto.

sentences.usage: Admitting a fault as well as reporting one. lo siento is what makes it an apology.
sentences.mnemonic: Broken is a state, and states are estar.

words.note: Takes a direct object with no preposition: ayudar a alguien takes an a only because it is a person. ayuda is also the noun, help.

sentences.trap: me climbs to the front of both verbs, exactly as M1 taught with ¿Me puede dar…?
sentences.sound: a-yu-DAR, with the y as in "yes" and the final r tapped once.

variations.changed: asked of a friend
the noun instead of the verb
offered rather than asked for, with M7's le

mistake.why: me never sits between two verbs. It goes in front of both: ¿Me puede ayudar?

sentences.usage: The sentence to have ready in any country. It works on a street, in a shop and at a counter alike.
sentences.mnemonic: The little word runs to the very front.

sentences.cue: I have to go to the doctor.

words.note: The dictionary form of voy, vas and vamos — a verb whose forms look nothing like it, which is why it has waited until it was needed.
Masculine or feminine by who the doctor is: el médico, la médica. Also used as the adjective medical.

sentences.trap: The que is obligatory. tengo ir is not a sentence, and English's "have to" gives no clue that a word is missing.
sentences.sound: IR is one syllable, and the r at the end is a single tap.

variations.changed: a place that takes no article

variations.cue: You have to go to the doctor.
variations.changed: said to a friend

variations.display: Tengo que quedar con mi hermana.
variations.cue: I have to meet my sister.
variations.changed: M6's verb inside the obligation

mistake.why: tener que needs its que: tengo que ir.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you have to leave, and the commonest excuse there is.

sentences.display: Perdone, creo que hay un error.
sentences.cue: Excuse me, I think there's a mistake.
sentences.literal: Excuse(polite), I-think that there-is a mistake.

words.note: Masculine: un error. Stressed on the second syllable, which is why the plural gains an accent nowhere — errores keeps the stress in the same place.

sentences.trap: Three softeners before the complaint even starts: Perdone, creo que, and un rather than el. Spanish does its complaining in the frame.
sentences.sound: e-RROR, with the double r rolled — a single tap would be a different word entirely.

variations.display: Perdone, creo que hay un problema.
variations.cue: Excuse me, I think there's a problem.
variations.changed: S09's noun in the same frame

variations.display: Disculpe, hay un error en la cuenta.
variations.cue: Sorry, there's a mistake in the bill.
variations.changed: M5's cuenta, and the place named
ser rather than hay, so it names rather than announces

mistake.why: hay never takes a definite article — M4's rule. And un keeps the complaint gentle.

sentences.usage: At a counter, a till or a table. It is the softest way in Spanish to say that someone has got something wrong.

sentences.display: Perdí la llave en la calle.
sentences.cue: I lost the key in the street.
sentences.literal: I-lost the key in the street.

words.note: perder in the past, and the accent is what makes it "I": perdí. Without it, perdi is nothing at all.
Feminine: la llave. The ll is a y sound, as in calle.

sentences.trap: The accent carries the person. perdí is I and perdió is he or she, and the only difference is which vowel wears it.
sentences.sound: per-DI, stressed at the end, which is what the accent marks. YA-be for llave.

variations.changed: the article where English wants a possessive

variations.display: Perdió la llave en el metro.
variations.cue: He lost the key on the metro.
variations.changed: the he-form, and the accent moves
plural, and a time from the level below

mistake.display: Perdi la llave en la calle.
mistake.why: Without the accent the word has no person and no stress: perdí.

sentences.usage: Reported to whoever might have found it. The past tense here is L1-M5's, doing exactly its job.

words.note: Masculine despite ending in -a: el problema, un problema. It belongs to a small Greek family — el tema, el sistema — and the ending predicts nothing.

sentences.trap: The word the whole course has been promising since its first gender note. If "-a is feminine" were a rule, this would be la problema.
sentences.sound: pro-BLE-ma, with the b soft between vowels and one tapped r.

variations.changed: the reassurance, which is how the word is most often used

variations.display: Hay un problema con el teléfono.
variations.cue: There's a problem with the phone.
variations.changed: hay announcing it, and con naming what it is with
M3's adjective, still agreeing masculine

mistake.why: problema is masculine: un problema. Learn every noun with its article and this never bites.

sentences.usage: Said about the situation rather than about the person, which is what keeps it civil.

sentences.cue: I can't find it, could you help me?

words.note: encontrar, and the stem changes o→ue like poder and doler: encuentro, encuentra, but encontrar.
The one place the little word may follow the verb: glued onto a dictionary form, as one word. ¿Me puede ayudar? and ¿Puede ayudarme? are both right and mean the same.

sentences.trap: Two legal places for me and no third. Either in front of everything, or glued to the end of a dictionary-form verb — never loose between them.
sentences.sound: en-KWEN-tro, with the ue glide again. a-yu-DAR-me, stressed where ayudar was.

variations.changed: the shortest it gets
the glued form standing alone
the thing named instead of pronounced

mistake.why: Loose between the verbs is the one place me cannot go. Either ¿Me puede ayudar? or ¿Puede ayudarme?

sentences.usage: In a shop, a station, an office. The two halves are a report and a request, and Spanish likes them in that order.
sentences.mnemonic: Front of everything, or glued to the end — nowhere in between.
